text:
The coalfields of eastern Kentucky fueled America’s economic rise in the early 20th century. But the state has since found itself left behind. A lack of investments in rural regions has triggered health and socioeconomic issues that have lingered for generations.
Today, Kentucky faces the third-highest cancer and third-highest drug overdose death rate in the country and is one of the top five worst-affected states in several other health metrics. It has come to rely heavily on federal healthcare assistance, with about 1.4 million people in Kentucky receiving Medicaid support.
But now, those issues are set to be further compounded by cuts to Medicaid enacted by the Trump administration that could directly affect up to 250,000 Kentucky residents.
About 35 rural Kentucky hospitals are believed to be at risk of closing as a result of the cuts, more than any other state.
“These hospitals are very dependent on Medicaid; it makes up a really significant part of the economy, particularly in eastern Kentucky. If you look at just Medicaid payments to providers in Kentucky’s 5th congressional district [a region encompassing much of Appalachian Kentucky], those payments make up 13.5% of the GDP there,” says Dustin Pugel, policy director at the Kentucky Center for Economic Policy, a research organization.
“That’s an enormous percent[age] of a regional economy. If that money starts to dry up either because people aren’t covered any more or through cuts to provider rates, that’s going to create enormous economic harm in those areas.”
Almost 36% of residents in Perry county in the south-east of Kentucky, including more than half of all children, relied on Medicaid in 2023 according to reports, a rate that’s 16% higher than the national level. At more than $10,600 per capita in 2023, Kentucky has some of the highest Medicaid expenses in the country.
The federal work requirement, in which many Americans must demonstrate they work or volunteer at least 80 hours a month in order to receive Medicaid support, comes into effect in January. Those who can’t submit records of hours worked or school attendance every six months will lose access from 2028. On top of that, reports suggests Kentucky is set to lose $28bn in federal Medicaid funding over the next decade.
Kentucky’s most vulnerable are set to be especially affected by the cuts. Local health centers, urgent care facilities and substance use disorder clinics that rely on federal funding to keep their doors open could face an untenable future.
“When you have five hospitals [in Appalachian Kentucky] that are at risk of closing, you have to take patients from an additional nine or ten counties. It’s going to overwhelm the hospital that’s here,” says Zack Hall, chair of the Perry County Democratic party.
“You already have a situation in eastern Kentucky where most counties don’t have a hospital.”
Hall says the two areas in Appalachian Kentucky that need a higher rate of healthcare have issues with cancer and black lung, which are harder on the elderly population.
“If you are having to take an elderly patient and bring them to the hospital and having to drive two, two-and-a-half hours to get them to a hospital, that makes it that much harder on them,” he says.
It stands to affect economies, not just individuals.
“In some of these counties, over two-thirds of their residents are covered by Medicaid. If they start losing coverage, particularly where there isn’t a lot of jobs – where people aren’t able to adhere to the work requirement or don’t have broadband so reporting their [work or volunteering] hours is difficult, you’re looking at a really significant economic headwind” says Pugel. “That will certainly result in layoffs, may result in hospital closures and will definitely hurt people’s health.”
Before the Trump administration shut down the refugee resettlement program to all but white South Africans last year, Kentucky ranked fourth nationally in refugee resettlements per capita, according to the Immigration Research Initiative.
Without immigration, which numbered nearly 82,000 people between 2020 and 2025, Kentucky would have seen its population decline.
But since last month, refugees and asylees, who have played an important role in revitalizing small Kentuckian communities in recent years, have lost access to Medicaid, because of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill.
From Covington, a city of about 42,000 people immediately south of Cincinnati, Wilson Mejia of Kentucky Refugee Ministries, a nonprofit with sites in three cities, has worked with about 840 refugees since opening the branch in 2021.
It used to receive funding from the Office of Refugee Resettlement, a federal agency. But under the Trump administration that has changed.
“That [funding] provided wraparound services for [refugees for] up to five years after arrival. Our case managers would help clients get access to social services [but] because of the changes with the Big Beautiful Bill, clients without green cards no longer have access to SNAP food services,” says Mejia.
“As of 1 October, clients that have not received their green cards can no longer access Medicaid. We are trying to work with the community to see where we can send these folks. But we are way off seeing the full impact of Medicaid changes. We anticipate it’s going to be a huge loss.”
For immigrants who do not have green cards and are charged with supporting family members, the health insurance marketplace is likely the only available avenue to securing health insurance. But the Trump administration has ended subsidies from the Obama administration’s Affordable Care Act, and insurance rates on the marketplace for 2027 are set to increase by about 42% compared to 2025.
Doctors and medical experts in Covington are volunteering to help refugees, but wider concerns remain.
“That income could have gone to rent, towards food. Now, it’s going towards medical coverage,” says Mejia, who adds that around 40-50 clients who have received letters about the ending of their Medicaid have sought help.
And for some immigrants who do hold a green card, meeting the 80-hours of work or volunteering per month requirement necessary to qualify for Medicaid may be near-impossible.
“Some clients can’t do this because they have a disability,” he says.
digest_he:
תוכנית הקיצוצים הנרחבת של ממשל טראמפ בתקציבי ה-Medicaid צפויה לגרום לפגיעה קשה באזרחים החלשים ביותר בארצות הברית, ובמיוחד במדינות עניות כמו קנטקי הנשענות במידה רבה על סיוע פדרלי לבריאות. השינויים הצפויים עלולים להשפיע באופן ישיר על כ-250 אלף תושבים במדינה ולהביא לסגירתם של עשרות בתי חולים כפריים.

בנוסף לדרישות עבודה חדשות ונוקשות המותנות בקבלת הסיוע, המדינות צפויות לאבד סכומי עתק במימון פדרלי לאורך העשור הקרוב. מצב זה יפגע אנושות במרכזים רפואיים מקומיים, במרפאות לטיפול בהתמכרויות ובשירותים חיוניים באזורים שבהם שיעורי המחלות והתמותה גבוהים במיוחד.

הקיצוצים פוגעים גם במהגרים ובפליטים אשר אינם מחזיקים עדיין בגרין קארד, ואיבדו את גישתם לשירותי בריאות מרכזיים בעקבות חקיקה חדשה. למרות מאמצים התנדבותיים של רופאים וארגונים מקומיים לסייע לנזקקים, מומחים מזהירים כי השלכות המדיניות יגרמו למשבר כלכלי ובריאותי חמור בקהילות רבות.
